speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chreiien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FURTHER GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN PANARCTIC OILS LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce today another major step in the development of Canada's north.
Members of the House will recall the announcement made on December 12, 1967, of the government's decision to enter into a unique partnership with 20 oil and mining companies to carry out a joint oil exploration and drilling program in Canada's Arctic islands through the creation of a new Canadian company, Panarctic Oils Ltd.
To finance the first stage of Panarctic's exploration program, costing $20 million, the federal government put up $9 million for a 45 per cent equity, and private capital $11 million for a 55 per cent equity.
Both government and industry recognized, at the time Panarctic was formed, that the program contemplated would require additional funds in the future. Each participant was given the right to extend his equity interest pro rata when the time came to increase the initial investment to $30 million or more.
Last fall Panarctic gave notice of its need to raise an additional $10 million and will give notice this spring of a need to raise a further $20 million to finance the next phase of its exploration activities in the Arctic islands.
The government recently reviewed the extent of its future involvement in Panarctic and whether it should retain its whole 45 per cent equity interest by investing in the next stage of the company's enlarged exploration and drilling program. Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to announce that the federal government will invest an additional $13.5 million in Panarctic Oils Ltd.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FURTHER GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN PANARCTIC OILS LIMITED
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FURTHER GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN PANARCTIC OILS LIMITED
speechtext:
The government will be
issued further preference and common shares in respect of its subscription, and this will maintain for the people of Canada its 45 per cent equity interest in Panarctic. This will bring the federal government's total investment in this daring and imaginative venture to $22.5 million.
Should Panarctic's program be further extended and additional capital be required above the present $50 million, the government retains the option of extending its interest pro rata. In addition, the agreement with Panarctic empowers the government to control the transfer of shares and, therefore, the degree of Canadian ownership and control in the company.
Maintenance of the government's 45 per cent equity in Panarctic will ensure for the people of Canada a direct interest in what promises to become Canada's largest oil company and a highly profitable business venture. And it will continue to provide for the original government objectives, namely, stimulation of oil and gas exploration in Canada's Arctic islands, maintenance of Canadian ownership and the control of the oil and gas rights over a very large sector of this potentially very rich oil basin, creation of employment opportunities for northern residents as well as other Canadians, and the development of Canadian technology suitable to northern terrain and climate.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Since Panarctic was formed the international oil industry has focused its eyes on the Arctic following the discovery of oil at Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, 200 miles west of the Yukon border. The recent oil discovery at Atkinson Point, 40 miles northeast of Tuk-toyaktuk in the Northwest Territories, has further accelerated interest in the Canadian north.
Exploration activity has increased remarkably in Canada's north since the start of Panarctic's operations. In early 1968, less than 190 million acres were held under oil and gas exploratory permit north of the 60th parallel. Today, more than 440 million acres are held under exploratory permit in this region. Expenditures on oil exploration in Canada's north were less than $25 million in 1967, rose

February 4, 1970
Panarctic Oils Limited to $45 million in 1969 and are expected to increase rapidly to an annual expenditure of $75 million by 1975.
The Arctic Islands, Mr. Speaker, are believed by many to be the most attractive oil basin in the world remaining to be explored. However, until major oil discoveries are made, Panarctic remains a high risk venture. The government has accepted this risk which clearly demonstrates its faith and commitment to northern development, as well as its determination to ensure active Canadian participation in the development of this last vast resource in Canada's last frontier-the Arctic Islands. The government's investment which I have the pleasure in announcing today is truly an investment in the bright and rich future of Canada's north.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FURTHER GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN PANARCTIC OILS LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in response to the statement of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. When the government first announced its intention to participate in this venture in 1967 the Hon. Alvin Hamilton, speaking on behalf of this party, endorsed it as a useful way in which the government of Canada could assist in the development of the north. We supported the proposal at that time, and I see no reason why we should take any different position now. It is a vehicle for northern development through which the Canadian people can participate to some extent in the profitable aspects of any development that takes place.
I think the minister might have been a little more cautious in referring to this enterprise as prospectively Canada's biggest oil company. This sounds a little like puffing and I think we should see our chickens before we start to count them. However, Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister's optimism is justified and I certainly wish the minister well. I am glad that the poor tired Minister of Finance is able to find this money, no doubt with great sacrifice to himself, in order to provide this additional support to the venture.
May I just say, Mr. Speaker, that I think the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development might interest himself a little in the pollution or preferably the antipollution practices followed by this company, because the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development drew to the attention of the House one or two rather unfortunate aspects of its work in the far north. I hope there will not be any more of this sort of thing but on the contrary that this company, of which the

government of Canada is a major shareholder, will set an example to all other companies operating in our northern environment.
In addition to its participation in this venture, I hope the government of Canada will recognize fully its responsibility in improving transportation in the north. One of the difficulties in northern development is the high cost of such development, and one of the reasons for the high cost, although not the sole one, is the high cost of transportation which does not appear to be highly organized in any respect. I take this occasion to remind the minister and the government as a whole of their obligation to improve transportation in the north. We are not going to see the sort of development we want to see in the north until there is adequate transportation there. There is no indication as yet that this government has fully recognized its responsibilities in this regard.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FURTHER GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN PANARCTIC OILS LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every Canadian is necessarily and unavoidably interested in the kind of development which is reported in our Arctic area. I want, on behalf of my party, to put on record some of our fears about the way this is being done and some basic objections to the way it is being done. We do not object to Panarctic being a consortium involving a large number of private corporations, but we do not see any reason at all why the government of Canada, and through it the people of Canada, should not have majority control in Panarctic instead of having .only 45 per cent control and 2 out of 12 directors on the board. I cannot understand the logic of that and the result has already begun to show, as I will indicate in a moment.
I am not at all certain that the exploration for oil in the Arctic is the best way to develop the north, that oil reserves are the greatest need for the people of Canada or, indeed, the people of the world in view of other oil reserves that are now available. I am not certain that the $20 million-odd spent by the government could not have been spent in some other way to assist the people living in the north. But if we are to spend this money, then surely we ought to be in total control of the operation, instead of only partial control.
The minister reminds us that the government has authority to authorize or to refuse to authorize the transfer of shares between various companies. That is true, Mr. Speaker. Despite that, as the minister well knows and as is shown in a background paper which I have read, Canadian ownership of the enter-
February 4, 1970

prise is now down to 70 per cent, whereas at the beginning it was somewhere around 90 per cent in Panarctic. Already the slide away from Canadian ownership to foreign ownership has begun. Furthermore, when you look at the background paper you will find that Panarctic is engaging in a method of farming out some of its operations in parts of its lands. A sentence in the background paper says, "In this respect Panarctic recently farmed out 945,000 acres of its various farm-outs jointly to Triad Oil Co., Ltd., and B.P. Oil Ltd.". I am sure the minister knows that Triad Oil Company Limited is a subsidiary of B.P. Oil Company Limited. Clearly, these lands are being farmed out to one corporation. The background paper then goes on to say, "These companies will jointly complete exploratory projects estimated to cost about $8 million and earn 50 per cent of Panarctic's interest in these lands."
There is a definite promise that Canadian ownership will be further eroded by this farming-out process that Panarctic conducts. It is that to which we, Mr. Speaker, of the New Democratic Party object. We see no reason why this natural resource should be handed over to foreign controlled companies, to a consortium of private corporations that are inter-related, that have members on each other's boards of directors, that own each other's shares and that have one single objective, to derive as much corporate profit and power as is possible. We see no reason why the Canadian government should not have invested in this corporation at least enough to give it 51 per cent control, in order that all the corporation's operations may be carried on in the public interest.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Let me make another point, Mr. Speaker. 1 will not be long because I know what the general rule is with regard to these statements. If I recall correctly, Mr. Speaker, the minister made the statement that the government is concerned with the creation of employment opportunities for the people in the north. It is significant and important to note that despite the concern of the government, only two or three native people are now being employed in the whole of the Panarctic operation. This is according to information which I have received. If an operation is going to be carried on in the north, particularly one that is not labour-incentive but capital-incentive, with only two or three native people employed, the concern of the
Labour Unrest at Quebec Ports government for the employment of northerners does not impress me very much.
Finally, I wish to emphasize the point made by the Leader of the Opposition on the problem of pollution. I summarize by saying that every time our country has had an opportunity to exploit and explore the great and rich natural resources of this country, we have leaped to give them away to the private corporations in this country and we have just as readily leaped to give them away to private corporations owned elsewhere. This, in our opinion, is a sell-out of the interests of the Canadian people and we wish to protest against it.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FURTHER GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN PANARCTIC OILS LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we can only rejoice at the progress and growth which this investment by the Canadian government is likely to spur. Still, we wonder about the wisdom of a decision to invest an additional $13.5 million in an undertaking which the minister describes as very risky.
The government ventured to invest $22.5 million in Panarctic Oils Limited, a decision which did not fail to surprise the people in certain areas of Quebec where mining and even oil resources are plentiful, because they realize that the paralysis which delays the development of these resources happens to result from a shortage of funds.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the question is: Should we spend millions of dollars to help a company whose economic viability is questionable, at a time when we are in the midst of an austerity program, as the Prime Minister never fails to remind us?
Let there be no mistake about it. If his department has millions to put in risk ventures, the minister should inform us accordingly, and we will be able to suggest to him some very good investments.
Mr. Speaker, we would like to know more about the terms and conditions of that agreement so that the population may assess its value.

subtopic: TABLING OF SMITH REPORT ON LABOUR UNREST AT QUEBEC PORTS
TABLING OF SMITH REPORT ON LABOUR UNREST AT QUEBEC PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to table in a few moments, in English and in French, what is known as the Smith report, a report of an
February 4, 1970

Labour Unrest at Quebec Ports inquiry into the abnormal causes of labour unrest at the ports of Montreal, Trois Rivieres and Quebec.
I wish to take this opportunity to make a brief statement and point out the terms of reference of this commission which, briefly stated, are as follows: to investigate conditions, conduct and matters not part of normal trade union activities, giving rise to labour unrest. These included such subject matters as pilferage, theft, and corruption. The terms of reference also included employer and business practices not part of or dealt with in collective bargaining but giving rise to labour unrest. These included methods of dealing with cargo at the ports, the methods of exercising discipline and the methods of maintaining a standard of good conduct. The full terms of reference may be found in the report which I am about to table.
The commission commenced its work in the autumn of 1968, after Mr. Justice Smith retired from the Court of Queen's Bench of Quebec. The commission presented to me, as Minister of Labour, its report in October of 1969 and since then the report has been translated, duplicated for distribution and is now being tabled.
On behalf of the government, I would like to thank the commissioner for the efforts he has made to deal with the problems he encountered during this lengthy and difficult inquiry. The inquiry grew out of the settlement of the stoppage of work in 1966 which tied up the St. Lawrence River ports for 38 days. It is encouraging to note that since the settlement of 1966, and more particularly since the recent three year contract signed in April of last year, there has been a marked improvement in labour relations in the port of Montreal. This year there has been no time lost through illegal work stoppage, and the collective agreement is being respected to a much greater degree than in previous years due, in no small part, to the work of Judge Alan Gold of Montreal, who acts as mediator and arbitrator of day-to-day problems in the port.
That there has been shown a greater responsibility on the part of the various union locals involved, as well as a serious effort on the part of management this year to deal with the unions through their newly formed Maritime Employers Association, should also be noted. Last week, the Canadian Importers Association indicated that the number of cases of pilferage reported had been reduced from 400 to 7, indicating that certain meas-

ures introduced in recent years by the National Harbours Board are proving effective.
I am also pleased to note that many of the recommendations of the report have already been implemented. Nevertheless, it would be unfair of me to leave the impression that labour-management regulations at the ports of Montreal, Trois Rivieres and Quebec do not leave much to be desired. The survival of these three important ports depends to a great degree on their ability to compete with similar ports in the United States, and a greater joint effort will have to be made in the future if these ports are to achieve their full potential.
A reading of the report will disclose that the Commissioner has been very critical of labour, management and port administration. The report is a very sobering document to which careful attention will have to be paid. While the government will take no action on any of the recommendations until all parties concerned have had an opportunity to give consideration to them and have made known their views with regard to them, it is my intention to implement as soon as possible those recommendations which the government thinks will improve industrial relations at the three ports, regardless of what temporary disruptive effects this may have on certain groups of employers or unions.

subtopic: TABLING OF SMITH REPORT ON LABOUR UNREST AT QUEBEC PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased to see that the minister has finally agreed to table in the House the Smith report which has been so long awaited not only by members of the House but also by all Canadians. I regret, however, that this report, which was submitted to the minister on October 2, should reach us three months later.
It should, I believe, be pointed out how difficult it is for opposition members, to submit their party's point of view about motions and reports the ministers table here, particularly when they are as bulky as the document that has just been tabled.
I therefore invite the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government house leader to give consideration to the feasibility of giving at least 24 hours' notice to opposition members before tabling reports or papers in the House. Members would then be able to go through the reports so as to criticize them in a positive and objective way.
February 4, 1970

This being said, I think that the government will want to examine the said report, in order to improve the administration of the nation's business. I can comment on some recommendations only in a very general way, but I feel that the Smith report does not show, at least at first sight, anomalies or facts which were not already known by those who closely followed the events which occurred in the above-mentioned ports.
I hope that the Smith report will not be a source of conflict or disagreement between the employees of the ports concerned, the unions, the owners and the users of those three main ports.
In addition, according to public opinion, the report would tend to emphasize among the general difficulties three specific conditions existing especially in the ports of Montreal, Quebec City and Trois Rivieres, while the government would have been wiser, in my opinion, to make comparative study of all Canadian ports and to relate them to port operations throughout the world, in the United States as well as in Europe. This would enable us to make a true evaluation of the port operations that are mentioned in the Smith report and of those occurring elsewhere. My reason for saying this is that some recommendations contained in the report are such that they question the honesty and efficiency of some workers, at those ports.
Since I represent a riding directly affected by those operations, I am in a position to say that most workers are conscientious and honest, although as it happens in all fields, there may be some questionable things going on.
I hope that the report will not be such as to aggravate or revive the difficulties that have already endangered relations between management and labour.
As I have stated, we cannot make a thorough examination of each of the recommendations on such short notice. For that reason, I take the liberty of pointing out that the report does not appear to give any thought to having, within a committee, a board of directors, or a local or national harbours board, representatives of the riverside municipalities that are directly affected by port operations.
I suggest that this is a glaring omission which the department should remedy.
I hope that the minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) will undertake to take action
Labour Unrest at Quebec Ports in order to assure the Canadian people that port operations will not be troubled again by local difficulties and that following their immediate and efficient action, ports will enjoy an economic activity beneficial to Canada as a whole.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Labour announces that a report he is tabling is a sobering document that is fair warning not to enter into an elaborate comment upon it until one has had an opportunity to study it. In the few minutes I have had to look at the report, I have come to agree with the position taken by the minister that it makes some far-reaching proposals which affect the three parties involved, namely labour, management and the port administration. I notice the minister has given the assurance- and I welcome it-that before any recommendations are implemented an opportunity will be given to these three parties to study the report and make their comments and their recommendations thereon. But I am glad to note the minister has recognized there has been an improvement in matters at the three ports as a result of the excellent work of Judge Alan Gold, as well as the fact that the union has taken a great deal of responsibility with respect to the things that take place at the ports, and the efforts of management in its dealings with labour.
We are glad to have the report tabled. As the minister says, it is a document which requires study. We welcome in particular the minister's statement that the three parties concerned will be able to make their recommendations to him before action is taken.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as mentioned by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey), the ports of Montreal, Trois Rivieres and Quebec were strikebound for 58 days in 1966. At that time, the government decided to institute a commission to study the problems that were leading to labour unrest in those ports as well as those which had nothing to do with regular union activities but which had caused discontent among workers. In fact, the latter had been involved in looting, theft and corruption.
It is undeniable that thieves operated in the ports of Montreal, Quebec and Trois Rivieres as is the case about everywhere. However, as the hon. member for Sainte-
February 4, 1970

Expansion of Airport Facilities Marie (Mr. Valade) was saying, the great majority of the employees in these ports are honest family men who work with courage and objectiveness.
This commission was therefore set up and went to work in 1968. In February 1970 the report is laid before us.
The minister stated a while ago and I quote:
It would be unfair of me to leave the impression that labour-management regulations at the ports of Montreal, Trols Rivieres and Quebec do not leave much to be desired. The survival of these three important ports depends to a great degree on their ability to compete with similar ports in the United States.
It is not a question of competing with Vancouver and San Francisco but with U.S. ports on the Pacific coast. The minister added and I quote:
A greater joint effort will have to be made in the future if these ports are to achieve their full potential.
It is evident that if it costs two or three times as much to use the ports of Montreal, Trois Rivieres and Quebec than that of Halifax or those on the U.S. coast, we will lose a lot. That is why, I think, the minister honestly appealed to employers and employees, particularly the unions, to behave objectively, to open their eyes and their ears, to approach the problem in a constructive way, in order to help the ports of Montreal, Trois Rivieres and Quebec, to win them patrons and to develop their facilities to the maximum.
In my opinion, the Smith report will help the parties concerned to better understand their responsibilities. Even if they assert their rights, they should not forget that they also have duties to discharge.
We have rights in every field. However, we also have duties that urgently need to be fulfilled. In this respect, trade unions, labour, management and the department are all considering together what has to be done to improve the situation, to prevent costly strikes in the future and to stabilize the economy in this particular field, which will enable workers and their families to foresee better days.

subtopic: TORONTO-REPORT ON PROGRESS IN PLANNING FOR EXPANDED FACILITIES

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: TORONTO-REPORT ON PROGRESS IN PLANNING FOR EXPANDED FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time I have been anxious to advise the House of the progress being made in connection with the De-

partment of Transport's over-all planning for expanded airport facilities to serve Toronto and the surrounding regions. From the outset we have been anxious to consult to the maximum extent possible with all of the parties who have a legitimate interest in this important project. I am referring to the province of Ontario, the municipalities in the area in question, and certain business and industrial interests.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
When the decision was made late in 1968 to seek alternative solutions to the original plan which was to expand the existing Malton airport a committee was established jointly with the government of Ontario, and this committee has been working most co-operatively ever since. From time to time we have sought means through which the other interested groups to whom I have referred could be made aware of the progress being made.
Hon. members will appreciate that this is not an easy task. At the outset, close to 60 different locations were involved as possible sites for the proposed airport. These regions are represented by more than 90 different municipalities. It can be seen, therefore, that worth-while consultation with such a very large group was not practical. This is especially true in view of the fact that the great majority of the locations were not in fact particularly desirable from a site standpoint and were therefore eliminated when the first of the long list of criteria was applied to them. As a result of this elimination process, it has now been determined that all but four or five of the sites considered originally are not usable. I want to emphasize that this does not mean that any or all of the sites still being considered will prove to be adequate. Much more investigation must be done on each of them before a final selection can be made.
Some indication of the complexity of the process of investigation can be obtained from the fact that such questions must be considered as passenger origin and destination studies, aviation technology, safety, ground transportation systems, noise capability, pollution, ecology, topography, economics and essential services such as water, sewage, power, etc. It is also essential that we take into account Ontario's long-range regional development plans and the effects of the proposed airport development on these. It can be seen, therefore, that a great deal of further study is necessary on the various potential sites still being examined.
February 4, 1970

Hon. members will appreciate that because of the risk of land speculation it is extremely important that there be no premature disclosure of the specific areas now under consideration. I appreciate that this necessity for secrecy is in conflict to some extent with our already expressed desire to consult as fully as possible with those other parties that have a very great and legitimate interest in this project. I feel, nevertheless, that there cannot be additional disclosure at this time. This view, I may say, is shared by the government of Ontario.
In the case of the so-called waterfront site the same considerations are not present, and therefore it has been possible for us to hold lengthy and detailed discussions with the city of Toronto, Metropolitan Toronto and the Toronto Harbour Commission. I can tell the House also for the reasons I have mentioned that while there will undoubtedly be some type of airport development along the waterfront at some time in the future it is now our judgment that this site is not appropriate for a full scale international airport. Rather, the downtown location is more likely to be developed as a facility limited to the accommodation of intercity and short-distance air traffic. I may say, too, that in so far as our planning for the waterfront location is concerned the various civic authorities to whom I have referred have representation on our technical subcommittees.
I anticipate that by fall of this year the necessary further investigations will have been completed, thus permitting the formulation of an airport system master plan for the Toronto and surrounding regions. At the earliest possible moment between now and then and as soon as it appears appropriate to do so, I am sure that the government of Ontario will agree with us to provide the fullest possible information to all interested parties. We are now exploring with the province the best approach to take in order to have a mutually advantageous exchange of information and views with the political, industrial and business communities.
If the House so wishes, Mr. Speaker, and presumably an opportunity will present itself when the main estimates are discussed, I will be pleased to appear before the Standing Committee on Transportation and Communications to elaborate on the contents of this statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter was just brought to my attention but that is not really too impor-

Expansion of Airport Facilities tant in any event because what was stated, of course, was a disclosure of the thoughts that all of us have in mind in regard to international airports. I believe the minister indicated in his closing words that he would be prepared to go into further detail in respect of the generalities and the nothingness in his statement.
One of the most important points in the minister's statement is the fact that there has been consultation. This is extremely important for the simple reason that we are now involved in considering amendments to our constitution. We have set up a joint committee on the constitution. It is extremely important that this continual dialogue or consultation, as the case may be, be regarded as of prime importance and always be a factor in the making of decisions. In other words, what I think is extremely important here is that the government has not acted arbitrarily.

The minister is now seeking information, through the province, from political and business interests as to the best way to approach this subject. It is most important, however, to obtain somehow a consensus of the views of the residents because it is they who may experience a great deal of frustration in terms of noise, land values and traffic.
I am pleased also that the minister is still interested in the waterfront, though not in terms of an international airport. But there should be a continuing dialogue with Toronto, Metropolitan Toronto, and also Hamilton harbour officials. This is the age of supersonic and jumbo jets. The minister should proceed with all due haste so Canada can play its role in this most important means of transportation, and so that he can make a further statement and, if at all possible, put his entire plans before the House by the fall.

subtopic: TORONTO-REPORT ON PROGRESS IN PLANNING FOR EXPANDED FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the representatives of the metropolitan area of Toronto I welcome the core of the minister's announcement. The core, as I found it, was that airport development along the waterfront in the east end of Toronto will not be for a large-scale international facility. This is no longer contemplated. The site should have been a non-starter from the word go. It is perfectly obvious to anyone
February 4. 1970

Expansion of Airport Facilities who knows the area that such a venture should have been rejected as unthinkable from the beginning, and probably would have been if the local people had been consulted. The noise pollution and the immense traffic problems that would have been created seriously would have depreciated the value of an attractive residential area which has been the home of many thousands of Canadians for more than 50 years.
The minister's statement refers to the civic authorities being represented on technical committees dealing with the proposed airport. The large urban areas and municipalities have responsibility for populations larger than some provinces. They must be made *effective planning partners at all stages of dealing with developments of this sort. If there are constitutional difficulties that must he overcome it may be impossible or impractical, as the minister's statement indicates, to deal with all municipalities concerned. But there is no reason why, in the consultation between the federal and provincially elected and politically responsible officials, members and representatives of the major municipalities affected should not be consulted.
I suggest to the minister that technical consultation is not enough. What is involved goes far beyond the question of airports; it concerns all the great problems of urban development facing us today.
The minister spoke of the danger of land speculation. I hope he will consult his colleague the Minister of Justice, who I believe will be able to inform him that under the Expropriation Act any effort to speculate in respect of expropriated land will probably be fruitless. If he will speak to the Minister of Finance and get an adequate capital gains tax we will not have to worry about such speculation at all.
I welcome the core of the announcement which will be received with relief by many of my constituents and other people in the city of Toronto. I hope that the process of consultation will continue and improve as time goes on.

subtopic: TORONTO-REPORT ON PROGRESS IN PLANNING FOR EXPANDED FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are always glad to listen to a statement made in the House about any kind of improvement. The statement made a few moments ago by the Minister of Transport

is one of those. Indeed, we can expect that there will be speculation, that consultations will take place and that the best possible site will be selected in order to improve Toronto's airport. On page 3 of the statement, I read these words, and I quote:

We are now exploring with the province the best approach to take in order to have a mutually advantageous exchange of information and views with the political, industrial, and business communities.

To my mind, the minister should have proceeded the same way with the government of the province of Quebec before selecting the St. Scholastique site. The Quebec government was consulted only after the decision had been taken and not before. Today we are told that discussions are taking place at the federal and provincial levels.
As regards the Montreal airport, the decision has already been taken. However, if there had been previous consultation with the provincial government, the Chambers of Commerce and intermediate bodies, that would have been fairer, more honest and sensible.
The statement further says, and I quote:

We are now exploring with the province-
Not without the province but with the province.
-the best approach to take in order to have a mutually advantageous exchange of information and views with the political, industrial and business communities.
And in this way to take a decision which will be shared by the province with Ottawa.

In my opinion, the same procedure should have been applied with respect to the St. Scholastique airport.
In any event, we are happy to see the government bring about some improvements in Ontario, in connection with the Toronto airport, and we congratulate the minister for consulting the organizations concerned, in short the population of that province, in order to find the most suitable site for the airport so as to control noise, air and water pollution, to the entire satisfaction of the population.
February 4, 1970

subtopic: AUTOMOBILE PRICE INCREASES
AUTOMOBILE PRICE INCREASES

subtopic: JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR WORKING POOR AND WELFARE CASES
JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR WORKING POOR AND WELFARE CASES
speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to increase the number of job opportunities as a key element in the program to assist Canada's working poor and hard-core welfare cases?

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Forest (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR WORKING POOR AND WELFARE CASES
speechtext:
Yes, in so far as the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is concerned.
The Department of Manpower and Immigration increases the number of job opportunities open to Canada's working poor and hard-core welfare cases primarily by making such persons more competitive in the labour market. In this way, their earning power is increased and their vulnerability to unemployment and underemployment is reduced.
The programs of the Department of Manpower and Immigration increase their productive skills, their employability, their knowledge of jobs and their mobility. The Canada Manpower Centres assist their placement in the labour force market or if unable to place them, refer them to training so that they can be better equipped to fill available employment opportunities. If employment is not available in their local community, it assists their movement to communities where employment is available to them. The Department is also supporting community agencies in experimental projects designed to assist poverty groups not normally reached by manpower services.
Using the Economic Council of Canada's definitions of poverty, the proportion of poor persons for whom the Department provides training is twice as high as the proportion of poor people to the population as a whole. In 1968-69, over $100 million was spent in the provision of training for such poor persons. The proportion of poor people, particularly with larger families is also higher among those helped under the Mobility Program, and almost all of the physically or mentally disabled per-
February 4, 1970

sons prepared for jobs through the Federal-Provincial Rehabilitation Program were poor and without employment. These programs continue to reach more persons each year and in 1969-70, the Department of Manpower and Immigration spent over $396 million in the manpower field alone to help people including a very substantial proportion on welfare or in poverty to find productive and worth while work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: YUKON PLACER MINING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOCATING OF CLAIMS, ETC.
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. This bill is relatively simple and straightforward, but I think I probably should take a few minutes in introducing the second reading of the bill to explain and outline what is proposed in this amending legislation.
This bill was passed by the other place on November 17, 1969, and after second reading in that place the bill was considered in the Senate Standing Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce and was reported back without amendment. Today, the placer mining industry in the Yukon does not have the importance it once held. As you know, Mr. Speaker, placer mining was at one time a thriving industry, particularly in the Dawson area, and represents an important and historic phase in the history of the Yukon. It is this phase that we intend to commemorate with the historic sites program to which I will refer in a moment.
February 4, 1970

Yukon Placer Mining Act From the period of 1897 to 1904, it is reported that the value of gold production exceeded $100 million. Most of this production was recovered by hand methods, such as pans, rockers and sluice boxes into which bold bearing gravel was shovelled and then washed. As transportation improved, thousands of tons of equipment were brought in and the scale of mining increased. Many claims were acquired and consolidated by corporations, with the individual miner being gradually replaced by large companies operating hydraulic and dredging plants. At one time, the Yukon Consolidated Gold Corporation had 9 dredges operating in the creeks in the vicinity of Dawson City. However, all dredging operations were closed down in the fall of 1966 when recovery of gold in this manner became uneconomic. Today, placer mining is conducted on a very small scale, comprising some 30 small one and two man operations, using bulldozers to push the gold bearing gravels into sluice boxes. Most of the creek beds in the Klondike area, where for the past 72 years placer mining was concentrated, have now been mined in one way or another. There is, of course, still some gold in the benches and in the hills, but it is extremely unlikely that further large-scale recovery of gold could be economical.
Under the Act which is proposed to be amended by this bill, the person staking a claim has all rights, not only to the minerals but all surface rights. The government does not even have the authority to set aside lands for roads, railways or pipeline rights of way, an historic site, national park, or any other public purpose. In the Yukon, all surface rights which have not been alienated for private purposes are still vested in the Crown in the right of Canada. All of these lands, at the present time, are now available to the placer prospector for claim staking. Under bill S-4, the government will have the authority where it feels there is a need for a road, airport, national park, or what have you for public purposes, to withdraw such lands as are required for such public purpose from the operation of the Yukon Placer Mining Act. Then, those lands could not be staked for placer mining purposes.
Of course, this legislation is not retroactive. In the case of existing claims under placer mining regulations, if the government required the land on which the claims were staked it would have to deal with the claim owner in the regular way by purchase or expropriation. Under the existing statute, 
which we propose to amend, only lands within the boundaries of a city, town, village, land occupied by a building, or forming part of an Indian reserve, are not subject to claim for placer mining purposes. I might give hon. members the following example of the application of the present law.
On November 1, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) announced in Whitehorse that the government had approved his recommendation for a $1.7 million historical sites program in the Yukon territory and also stated that the government had reached an agreement with the Yukon Consolidated Gold Corporation to purchase the "Gold Room" now located at the company's establishment at Bear Creek near Dawson City and which the government, through the department, proposes to move to Bonanza creek. There is already a commemorative plaque erected near the site of the "discovery claim" and a considerable amount of public funds have been spent in maintaining this site. As previously stated, there is no provision in the Act to protect such lands from its application.
Considering, therefore, the limited extent of the industry to-day, the amendments proposed in the Bill are of minor significance. As I have mentioned, these proposals are not retroactive and cannot, therefore, affect existing rights. As hon. members know, after second reading the bill will, of course, be referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Of course, hon. members of the committee will have an opportunity, if they wish, to examine this measure in more detail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in introducing the bill the parliamentary secretary was, in effect, telling the House that there is no more gold in "them thar hills". I suppose this is one way of announcing the passage of an era that made Canada famous around the world at the time the original rush to the Klondike occurred. I am not sure that one should feel he is optimistic in hoping there might yet be some places within the boundaries of the Yukon or in some other part of Canada where the kind of activity that is characteristic of a placer gold mining rush might again occur.
The bill, as it is proposed, should find general acceptance by members of the House because it does meet some of the situations which arise, other than historic ones, in respect of placer mining in the Yukon. Mr. Speaker, I take it my hon. friend heard my remarks a moment ago and that he can understand them as well as anyone. They are on record in Hansard. I say to the hon. member that I did not intend to leave the impression that the remarks meant anything more than what the plain, ordinary sense of them on reading will indicate.
As I said before the interjection of the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, members have had an opportunity now for some time to read Bill C-152. I would like to say something about the bill and the reason we are asking Parliament at this time to amend the National Parks Act.
During the past few years the rate of social, economic and technological change has increased the complexity of administering Canada's national parks. Visitation to the parks has increased tremendously and is continuing at the rate of approximately 10 per cent per year. In addition to the basic requirement for additional visitor accommodation in the parks, the increased visitation has also underlined the need for many new national parks and for rationalization of the use that is made of existing parks. In other words, it has become more important than ever before to ensure that our parks are used consistent with the best national interest.
The department's leasehold policy, covering both private dwellings and commercial estab-

lishments in the national parks has gone a long way to ensure that private interests in the national parks do, in effect, serve the needs of the nation and the visiting public. Under departmental policy, persons in business or employed in the parks may reside there. Commercial leases are granted only where, in the minister's opinion, there is a need for this or that particular visitor service. Assignment and reassignment of leases are controlled by the department. Also under our policy, the duration and conditions of leases, and particularly commercial leases, must be such that full control is exercised by the government, on behalf of the people of Canada, on what services are provided, where they are provided, how they are provided and for what duration.
There is yet another aspect of our policy dictated by the underlying principle that national parks are public lands held in trust for the benefit, enjoyment and education of all Canadians. That aspect, Mr. Speaker, is the question of financial return to the Crown as a result of private commercial activity in the parks. Such activity thrives and grows, to a very large extent, by virtue of the very presence of the parks and the millions of dollars invested by the Canadian taxpayers in their acquisition and development. Consequently, it is important that there be a commensurate financial return from the commercial opportunities offered within the parks.
The point I wish to make here, Mr. Speaker, concerns not only the merits of our policy, but the need to choose the best instrument available to implement the policy. The minister thought it important to show, in a general way, how our policy is essential to the best use of Canada's national parks. I now want to show in more detail how and by what instrument this policy can best be applied. The instrument that is being proposed is the National Parks Leaseholds Corporation. The institution of this corporation is the main object of Bill C-152. The bill also deals with several other matters that I shall mention later.
The National Parks Leaseholds Corporation is conceived as a commercial Crown corporation to administer all leases in the national parks and those public park lands intended for commercial uses that may be entrusted to its management. It is not intended that the corporation engage itself in any way in the administration or management of park lands as such, or what may be more generally described as "green areas". We are convinced that a commercial organization is indeed best
February 4, 1970

National Parks Act
suited to administer what are essentially commercial interests. However, it must be a publicly owned commercial organization, accountable to the government and ultimately Parliament, because it will serve objectives that must be consistent with the purposes of national parks and more generally with the best public interest.
The establishment of the Leaseholds Corporation will have an important effect on the national parks administration. It will free the parks organization from the complex and specialized business of commercial property management, thereby enabling it to concentrate its efforts on the planning, development and preservation of national parks. Bill C-152, in so far as it concerns the National Parks Leaseholds Corporation, provides for the constitution, organization, financing and the powers of the corporation. The objects and powers of the corporation are such that it will be able to assume the control and management of such public lands in the parks, and of such commercial facilities within the parks as may be entrusted to it.
The powers of the corporation will be sufficiently broad to enable it to construct and operate commercial facilities in the parks or alternatively to arrange for the construction and operation of such facilities if it so chooses. The intention here is that the corporation be in a position to satisfy the requirements of the parks for visitor services in the most advantageous way within the context of the National Parks Act and Regulations. Thus, development could range from construction and operation by a lessee, through a partnership arrangement with the corporation to a situation where a facility is constructed and operated by the corporation itself.
In the latter regard, there have been and presumably will continue to be, instances where there is a need for visitor service facilities but where economic and/or social conditions are not conducive to an investment by the private sector of the economy. I am reminded of at least two instances in the relatively recent past, Terra Nova Bungalows, Terra Nova National Park and the Alpine Chalets and Motel, Fundy National Park, where a demand existed for public accommodation but where the prospective rate of return on an investment by the private sector was such that no one could be interested in fulfilling this demand. In these two instances, the department financed the construction of the required facilities and, in due course, leased them to private groups for their operation.
In all matters assigned to it, the corporation will operate within the context of the National Parks Act and regulations, and such other governing legislation as may apply. In the discharge of its responsibilities, the corporation will, with the approval of the Governor in Council and in respect only of limited estates or interests in public lands in the parks, have the powers of the Crown as provided for in the Expropriation Act. Thus, the corporation's powers of expropriation are less than those now available to the minister. The right of expropriation will enable the corporation to assemble public lands in the parks for redevelopment purposes or to extinguish, with compensation, certain rights previously conveyed by the Crown.
The corporation will be subject to legal recourse by its lessees, agents, contractors, or the general public; in other words, it may sue or be sued in any court that would have jurisdiction if the corporation were not an agent of Her Majesty.
It is intended that the corporation be allowed to borrow money from private sources at its discretion. Under such circumstances, however, these loans would not be guaranteed obligations of the government of Canada. This authority precludes the necessity of the corporation looking to public funds for such things as short term borrowings, working capital requirements, etc.
The financial provisions of the bill enable the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to make loans to the corporation on terms and conditions approved by the Governor in Council. Such loans cannot exceed $20 million in aggregate. The corporation will be able, however, to borrow money from other sources, thus precluding the necessity for it to come back through government machinery for capital. This will provide the flexibility and initiative necessary for the corporation to develop, within the limits of what is appropriate in a park, all of the commercial possibilities with a maximum return to the corporation.

While the corporation must have considerable latitude in these and other matters, it will not have unlimited scope. The control of capital and operating budgets, as provided under section 80 of the Financial Administration Act, will apply. In other words, it is envisaged that the Leaseholds Corporation will function in a budgetary control sense in the same way as the Northern Canada Power Commission, Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and

February 4, 1970
National Parks Act
others. Also, Treasury Board may establish the maximum amount in terms of the Corporation's gross receipts that it may spend annually for administration purposes. I particularly want to emphasize that while the corporation should have as much freedom as possible in the conduct of its business, it will by law be restricted to enterprise that is consistent with the purposes for which the parks are dedicated. Inasmuch as the corporation will be subject to the National Parks Act and regulations, and inasmuch as the Governor in Council and the minister retain the right to remove from the corporation's control any lands or facilities, the minister will always have the authority necessary to control the activities of the corporation in all parks.
The net earnings of the corporation will be credited to a fund to be known as the Parks Development Fund. This fund will be used by the corporation in the conduct of its business. Provision is made whereby the Governor in Council may establish the maximum amount that the Parks Development Fund may contain, and earnings in excess will be deposited in the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to summarize the remaining aspects of Bill C-152. The bill provides authority for members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to collect volun ary penalties for infractions of the National Parks Highway Traffic Regulations. Present regulations require that traffic violations be heard before a court of law. In many cases, this represents delays and inconvenience to visitors, especially to those who live far from the park and who are travelling on a schedule.
The bill also provides for new legal descriptions of Banff, Jasper, Waterton Lakes, Yoho, Kootenay, Mount Revelstoke, Prince Albert, Riding Mountain, Georgian Bay Islands and Prince Edward Island National Parks. As well, it provides for the deletion of Fort Beausejour Historic Park and Fort Anne Historic Park from the schedule of national parks. It is proposed that these two parks be set aside as national historic parks by the Governor in Council pursuant to section 10 of the National Parks Act.
The amendment further provides for a legal description of Terra Nova National Park in Newfoundland to be added to this schedule. When Terra Nova was proclaimed a national park on May 11, 1957, a legal survey under the Canada Lands Surveys Act had not been completed. The legal description should now be included.
[Mr. Woolliams.l
Bill C-.152 also provides for the establishment of a national park in the area of Kejim-kujik Lake in Nova Scotia. Since 1963, negotiations have been taking place with the Province of Nova Scotia for the establishment of a second national park in that province. Agreement has been reached with the province on the boundaries of the proposed park and the province has made the land available, free of all encumbrances. The area of the new park, to be known as Kejimkujik National Park, is approximately 145 square miles.
The bill further provides legislative authority for the Governor in Council to add, from time to time, Crown-owned lands to the national parks. Under the existing legislation, additional lands acquired for park purposes can only be added to the schedule by amending the National Parks Act. Until such amendment is made, the lands cannot be managed under the authority of the act or regulations. Bill C-152 will enable such new lands to be brought under the National Parks Act and regulations by order in council. While the amendment will facilitate the addition of lands to the system, an act of Parliament will continue to be required before any lands may be removed.
I have to thank hon. members for allowing me this opportunity to introduce the bill on second reading. When it has been given second reading it will, of course, be referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Interested people-and I know that a considerable amount of interest has been shown in this legislation, particularly by those in the parks area-will have an opportunity to appear before the committee as, of course, will senior officials of the department.

Members over on that side do all their talking from their seats. I have a great deal more to say on this subject.
This whole performance, this whole effort to play down the bill in front of us, may have something to do with the manner in which the minister was received when he was out visiting the national parks area of Banff and Jasper recently after he had addressed his wellknown admoni ion to the leaseholders out there: If you don't like it, get off the property; go east, go west, but don't stay here. This whole attitude is typical of what we have seen in the last few months in this Parliament.
As I say, this bill was announced as one of the great pieces of legislation to be presented to Parliament this session, though, of course, the government must have changed its mind in this regard because they do not seem to be treating it now with the importance they had previously ascribed to it. What does it do? It makes some relatively minor adjustments in the boundaries of the national parks, reducing the size of most of them, from what I have been able to gather. What else does it do? In a nutshell, it sets up a corporation to carry out the administration and to make policy for the national parks. If ever I saw a glorious, grand and blatant opportunity for patronage, this is it.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
This is a deceptive bill. At first glance it does not appear to give an unwarranted degree of power to the National Parks Leasehold Corporation. The object of the bill, apparently, is to put into the hands of the corporation the day to day management of the properties of the federal government in its national parks. As the parliamentary secretary put it, this would have quite an effect on the management of the parks. I think that is putting it mildly. The bill is drafted in such a vague manner that in practice the powers to be exercised by the corporation may be considerable. There are many examples of such dangerous vagueness. I know it is not the custom at this stage of a bill to go into the detail of the clauses. I do not propose to do so, other than to illustrate the point that the bill is very deceptive and vague. In my view it is purposely drafted to mislead members of the House into voting for something for which they would not otherwise have voted. One example is new section 15(1) which reads:
The objects of the Corporation are to develop, manage and maintain, on a basis that is economically sound and consistent with the purposes for which the National Parks are dedicated, property in the Parks the direction of the administration, management and control of which is entrusted to it.
Who is to decide what is an economically sound basis? What will be the situation if the public does not agree with what the corporation thinks on this question? Is the corporation itself to decide what is consistent in respect of the purposes of the national parks? What can be done should a citizen feel that the corporation's interpretation in this regard leaves something to be desired?
Another example of excessive vagueness is new section 15(2)(b) which states that the corporation may lease or otherwise make available on a commercial basis and subject to such terms and conditions as it considers necessary or desirable any property under its control. Again, this would seem to involve a rather wide authority. Presumably, the corporation could grant leases in such a way as to nullify zoning regulations in the parks. If it should set such lax terms in respect of leases that shoddy buildings are erected in the midst of great natural beauty, what can be done. There are a great many more sections to which I could refer. However, I think this might more properly be done before the committee.
I am concerned about new section 20 (1) which says that no by-law shall come into

February 4, 1970
National Parks Act
force until it is approved by the Governor in Council. Here we have a lovely situation. For all practical purposes, the administration and policy in respect of our parks is to be turned over to a Crown corporation. This is similar to the situation of a few years ago when, in respect of transportation, the power of this Parliament was removed and placed under the Canadian Transport Commission. In this case, the government is attempting to have the best of both worlds. It is setting up a corporation with a president, a vice-president and five directors.

My colleague says that is the musical ride. I would call it a musical snow job. There are quite a number of other items here .on which I might comment. We have seen government press reports and have heard rumours to the effect that the minister hopes to undertake a vast program of expansion of our park system so that the land area encompassed in national parks will be doubled in ten years. Such reports also indicate that the minister plans to develop a series of non-wilderness parks located close to centres of heavy population and suited to intensive public use. It would seem from this bill that so far as actual parks are concerned, all the government is doing is altering the boundaries of existing parks so that there will be a net loss of park area. The bill is a downright dangerous piece of legislation in so far as the provisions for a leasehold corporation are concerned. The granting of power is extremely poorly defined. Secondly, where the granting of power is clear it is also clear that the corporation will have responsibilities in 
respect of what amount to policy making activities.
I say that this is a dangerous and repugnant situation with regard to the administra* tion of our parks. The corporation is given power under section 95 (2) (b) to lease or make otherwise available on a commercial basis, and subject to such terms as it considers necessary or desirable, any property under its control. But the power to set the conditions of leases is the power to set over-all policy for the parks and to effect to a large extent the way in which the parks are developed. Suppose, for example, the corporation should decide, as the parks department has in recent years, to offer no guarantee to commercial leaseholders that their leases will be renewed or even that they will receive compensation for capital improvement to the land. This caii only encourage the commercial developers to adopt a get rich quick attitude. Scalping of tourists is likely to result.
There are a great many other things with which I should like to deal. However, a number of other members of the House I and informed are anxious to speak on this bill. Many of them represent areas in which there are national parks. These members will wish to discuss in great detail the many complaints, fears, worries and apprehensions people have as a result of this bill. When the time comes my colleagues and I -will certainly find it necessary to vote against this legislation. In our opinion it is a bad bill. It simply provides an opportunity to the government to evade its responsibility by establishing a corporation behind which it may hide. This corporation will be able to do what it likes in respect of leases and conditions of leases. It is such a blatant example of potential patronage I am surprised the government would bring it before the House. I suppose one becomes bolder and bolder as time passes.
More important from a long range point of view is the fact that for all practical purposes this bill would take the administration of our national parks virtually out of the control of Parliament. This is another example of what this government has been doing and which its immediate predecessor has done for a number of years. It has cut down the power and responsibility of Parliament. The government would appear to have one particular desire. I am not referring to government backbenchers. They have been very conscientous in committee work and in respect of matters such as this. I am referring to the members of the treasury benches. The intention would appear to be to cut down the responsibility of
February 4, 1970

this House and the effective participation of members in the running of our country. This is being done consistently all the time. It is another example, if this activity is not stopped, of the fact that by the time this government's term of office has expired there may not be any use for this House at all.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I have heard the comment that the motto of this government is peace, power, patronage and perpetuity. If ever there was an example of this motto, this is it. As I mentioned earlier, the members of this party take great exception to the way this bill has been presented to the House. The minister has other engagements and I am not questioning the importance of those engagements. What I am objecting to is the way the business of this House is run by the government and the house leader. It is so bad that provision is not made to have the responsible minister in the House to present important legislation.
Possibly there is an excuse for the minister's absence this afternoon. We are told that all day tomorrow as well, the minister will be gallavanting, or perhaps attending to important business, out west visiting Indian reservations. There is just no excuse for this. It is the minister's duty to be in the House when measures as important as this are presented. No one would object or complain about his absence. What we are complaining about is the fact that when this major piece of legislation is presented he is not here. Representatives of his department are here, but he has responsibility for the bill. I think the minister should return to his duties. We are not prepared to continue the debate on this motion until he does return.
For this reason I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale), that this House do now adjourn.
